You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Deliver 4.5V to 5.5V at node `out` under six conditions (S1-S6).
    *   Constraints:
        *   `vavg >= 4.5V` (min supply)
        *   `vmax <= 5.5V` (abs max)
        *   `vpp <= 0.05V` (low ripple)
        *   `tup <= 0.4s` (fast cold start)
        *   `dv <= 0.02V` (settled mean)
    *   Piezo source: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30 nF) and 20 MΩ leakage. Open circuit voltage $V_{OC} \approx 3.8\text{V}$.
    *   Key issue from previous rounds:
        *   `SSHI_FBR` ([c0075]) is close but:
            *   Over-voltages on S1, S3, S5 (S3 reaches 12.2V!).
            *   Under-voltages on S4 (3.78V) and S6 (4.15V).
            *   Need a way to limit voltage and boost performance on weak conditions.

    *   SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) with a Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR).
    *   SSHI increases the harvested energy by flipping the voltage across the piezo capacitor $C_p$ at the peaks of the displacement.
    *   The FBR then converts the AC voltage to DC.
    *   The current best design [c0075] is almost there for S2 but fails S3 (too high) and S4/S6 (too low).

    *   *Over-voltage on S3:* The load $R_L$ is very high (10 MΩ), and $I_p$ is high (120 uA). We need a voltage clamp to keep `out` $\le 5.5\text{V}$.
    *   *Under-voltage on S4/S6:* The current is too low (40 uA on S4) or the load is too heavy. We need higher efficiency or a slightly higher "effective" output voltage.

    *   *Clamping:* A Zener diode (DZ33) isn't enough since it clamps at 3.3V. We need a clamp at 5.5V. However, the prompt says we have DZ33 (3.3V Zener). We can't easily make a 5.5V Zener.
    *   *Alternative Clamping:* Use a series diode to shift the Zener clamp? No, the Zener is between `out` and `0`. If I put a diode in series with the Zener, the clamp voltage is $V_z + V_{forward}$. $3.3\text{V} + 0.7\text{V} = 4.0\text{V}$ (too low). $3.3\text{V} + 0.25\text{V} = 3.55\text{V}$ (too low).
    *   Wait, maybe the Zener is used elsewhere? Or maybe we use a different topology that naturally limits the voltage.

    *   The SSHI is already very efficient. The problem on S4/S6 might be the diode drops of the FBR.
    *   FBR has 2 diode drops in the path from piezo to storage. $2 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$.
    *   Can we use a Synchronous Rectifier (using switches)?
        *   The prompt allows 2 SYNC controllers and 4 switches.
        *   SSHI already uses 1 SYNC and 1 switch for the inversion.
        *   If we use the second SYNC for rectification, we can reduce the voltage drop.

    *   The problem with [c0075] is that it's "too strong" for S3 and "too weak" for S4/S6.
    *   Wait, looking at [c0075] results:
        *   S3: `vavg` = 12.2 V.
        *   S4: `vavg` = 3.78 V.
        *   S6: `vavg` = 4.15 V.
    *   The output voltage depends heavily on the load $R_L$. Since $R_L$ varies from 1 MΩ to 10 MΩ, a simple passive storage capacitor won't keep the voltage between 4.5 and 5.5 V.
    *   We need a way to regulate the output. Since we don't have an active regulator (like a buck/boost converter with a feedback loop), we must rely on:
        1.  A shunt regulator (Zener).
        2.  Tuning the SSHI parameters.
        3.  A different rectifier topology.

    *   Can we use a Zener clamp to keep S3 under 5.5V?
        *   The available Zener `DZ33` is 3.3V.
        *   If we put `DZ33` on `out`, `vout` will be $\approx 3.3\text{V}$, which is below the 4.5V minimum.
        *   What if we use the Zener as part of a charge pump or in a different location?
        *   Wait, if we use a voltage doubler *after* the SSHI, we might get more voltage for S4/S6, but S3 will be even higher.

    *   The FBR (4 diodes) is used for rectification.
    *   Current SSHI uses $L_1$ and $S_1$ for inversion.
    *   Maybe a Half-Bridge Rectifier (HBR) would be better? (Reduced diode drops).
    *   Wait, if the piezo is floating (pzp, pzn), a full bridge is typical. But if pzn is connected to ground through a capacitor, we can use a half-bridge.

    *   If we use a synchronous rectifier instead of diodes for the main path, we eliminate the $\sim 0.5\text{V}$ drop.
    *   Proposed structure: SSHI with synchronous rectification.
        *   SYNC G1: Inversion (as before).
        *   SYNC G2: Rectification.
        *   Wait, the rectification happens at the same time as the energy transfer.
        *   Standard SSHI: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Rectifier $\rightarrow$ $C_{out}$.
        *   The rectifier is always on. The inversion switch $S_1$ is pulsed.
        *   If we replace the FBR diodes with switches, we need a way to control them. But we only have 2 SYNC controllers.
        *   G1 for inversion. G2 for... what?
        *   Maybe we can use G2 to pulse a switch that acts as a "dump" or "clamp"?

    *   Let's look at the "SSHI_FBR" results again. S4 and S6 are just below 4.5V (3.78V and 4.15V).
    *   The drop is small. Maybe we can increase the efficiency of the rectification.
    *   Instead of a Full Bridge, can we use a center-tapped like structure? (Not possible with the piezo model).
    *   What about a "Synchronous SSHI" where the rectifier is also switched?
        *   In a typical SSHI, the inductor $L$ is used to flip the voltage.
        *   If we use the switches $S_2, S_3$ to replace the diodes $D_1, D_2$ (the ones going to `out`), we can reduce the drop.
        *   G2 could control $S_2$ and $S_3$. But $S_2$ and $S_3$ need to be closed at different times (positive vs negative half-cycle).
        *   Wait, `edges="both"` closes the switch for `ton` at both peaks.
        *   If we have $S_2$ and $S_3$ in parallel with the rectifier diodes, we could potentially lower the drop. But $S_2$ and $S_3$ can't be controlled independently by one SYNC.

    *   S3 is 12.2V. This is way too high.
    *   The load is $R_L = 10 \text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   We need to bleed off excess current.
    *   An `R_bleed` resistor (like in `SSHI_FBR_Bleeder`) helps, but it also lowers the voltage for S4.
    *   We need a non-linear bleeder. A Zener diode is non-linear.
    *   Wait! If we use a Zener in series with a resistor? Or a Zener in parallel with a capacitor?
    *   If we use two Zener diodes in series: $3.3\text{V} + 3.3\text{V} = 6.6\text{V}$.
    *   A clamp at 6.6V might be too high (vmax <= 5.5V).
    *   What if we use a Zener and a Schottky diode? $3.3\text{V} + 0.25\text{V} = 3.55\text{V}$. Still too low.

    *   S4: $I_p = 40 \mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 4.7 \text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   S6: $I_p = 60 \mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 2.2 \text{ M}\Omega$.
    *   In these cases, the output is just under 4.5V.
    *   Maybe the issue is the $L$ value or the `ton` timing in the SSHI.
    *   But the automatic tuner already tried to optimize those.

    *   If the FBR is the bottleneck (0.5V drop), and we can't use synchronous rectification for everything...
    *   What if we use a different rectification topology?
    *   A voltage doubler? (FB_Doubler failed the screen).
    *   What about a "Half-Bridge" with a large capacitor to ground?
        *   Piezo pzp $\rightarrow$ Diode $\rightarrow$ `out`.
        *   Piezo pzn $\rightarrow$ Capacitor $C_{mid} \rightarrow$ 0.
        *   This replaces the 4-diode bridge with a 2-diode bridge (or even 1 diode if configured correctly).
        *   Actually, a standard "half-wave" SSHI:
            *   $C_p$ is flipped.
            *   Only the positive peak is harvested: $pzp \rightarrow D \rightarrow out$.
            *   Wait, that's less power.

    *   Let's try a "Voltage Doubler" inspired approach but keep the SSHI inversion.
    *   Actually, let's try to improve the SSHI_FBR by adding a "clamping" mechanism that is more effective than a simple resistor.
    *   Wait, if I can't use a 5.5V Zener, can I use a capacitor and a switch to dump energy?
    *   `S2 S out n2 ctrl=G2`, `R2 R n2 0 1e+05`, `G2 SYNC ...`
